\chapter{Review --- All Four Stem Changes}
\label{ch:spanish-review-stem-changes}
\hlchaptermodality{166}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name all four stem-change patterns and the single verb that owns one of them.}

The system closes at four - and u-to-ue has exactly one member.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — the four stem changes, all of them}

\label{lesson:ES-C39-repaso-cambios}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Say a verb whose stem breaks under stress — any one you have met.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Something finished in the last two chapters and it is worth stopping for.

Spanish has \textbf{four} stem-change patterns. Not five, not a dozen — four. You met the first two long ago with \emph{querer} and \emph{poder}, and the last two in the chapters you have just finished. That is the whole system, and you now hold all of it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the change} & \textbf{the verb that taught it} & \textbf{what breaks} \\
\midrule
\textbf{e $\to$ ie} & \emph{querer} & $\to$ \emph{quiero} \\
\textbf{o $\to$ ue} & \emph{poder} & $\to$ \emph{puedo} \\
\textbf{e $\to$ i} & \emph{conseguir} & $\to$ \emph{consigo} \\
\textbf{u $\to$ ue} & \emph{jugar} & $\to$ \emph{juego} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This table is allowed here because every row in it is something you can already do. It is a picture of the ground you hold, not a list to memorise.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pattern with one member}]
The fourth row is strange, and worth knowing precisely.

\textbf{u $\to$ ue happens in exactly one verb in the entire language: \emph{jugar}.}

Not \textquotedblleft{}mostly one.\textquotedblright{} One. Every other Spanish verb with a \emph{u} in its stem leaves it alone. So you are not learning a pattern here so much as a single fact with a pattern's shape — which is easier, not harder, and is the kind of thing a course should tell you instead of letting you brace for more.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item one verb from each of the four rows
  \item the four changes themselves, as sounds — \emph{e-ie, o-ue, e-i, u-ue}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until naming the pattern is faster than working it out.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many stem-change patterns are there? (\textbf{Four} — and that is all of them.) Which one has a single member? (\textbf{u $\to$ ue}, only \emph{jugar}.) Next chapter is not about forms at all — it is about three places where English gives you one word and Spanish makes you choose.
\end{tcolorbox}
